coverNote: This is the short edition: every diagram, the bottlenecks that matter most, one card per theme and one table of the work packages. Start with “The short version” and Part 4. The reference edition, `HARNESS-IDEAS-AND-BOTTLENECKS-2026-11-13-REFERENCE.pdf` beside this file, holds every idea, every bottleneck and every package card in full. Every number carries a tag that says how sure we are of it.
howLead: This is the short edition of the one place where everything we have learned about our build harness sits together. It keeps every diagram and gives what a teammate needs to pick a piece of work, see why it matters and see what has already been tried. The reference edition, `HARNESS-IDEAS-AND-BOTTLENECKS-2026-11-13-REFERENCE.pdf` beside this file, holds every idea, every bottleneck and every package card in full. Throughout, “I” is me and “we” is the team.
howIds: **Ideas** are numbered by theme: `MAC-03` is the third idea in the machine theme. Part 3 has a card for each of the twelve themes.

**Bottlenecks** keep the ids given by the session that found them. `B01` to `B21` come from the bottleneck compile of 11 November. `R2`, `R4` and `B3-LOOP` are loops of harness v2 (Part 1) that are bottlenecks in their own right. Ids that start with `TK` (tokens), `LIB` (memory), `MC` (the machine and the check) or `PR` (process; not a pull request) were added in this compile.
**Loops** are written “loop R1” or “loop B2”. R marks a loop that feeds itself, B a loop that pushes back toward a limit.

**Work packages** are `WP1` to `WP11`. **Decisions** waiting on me are harness v2’s `D05` and `D07` to `D23`, the knowledge store’s `KS-D1` and `KS-D1b`, and named ones such as `GT-1`; Part 4 lists them all.
**Terms** are explained in the text, or in the glossary with where each comes from.
shortLead: I build software with AI agents. The harness is everything around them: how I split work into sessions, the checks that decide whether work is right, the memory that carries what we learn, the PC it all runs on, and how results come back to me. For two weeks we studied that harness directly: what slows it down, what each fix could be worth, and which outside ideas are worth borrowing. This edition gives that record in brief, and it ends with the work split into packages people can own.
ask: **What I need from you.** Read this page and Part 4, take a package (two people can share one) and write your name in its row. Parts 2 and 3 give the background for your package, and the reference edition holds every bottleneck and idea behind it.

p1.lead: FixFlow is the product. The harness is how we build it: everything we wrap around the AI models to build software with them. The word comes from software testing, where a test harness is the code that runs the tests; teams that build with AI agents now use it for the whole system around a model.
harness: **Sessions and agents.** A session is one conversation with Claude Code, Anthropic’s coding tool, which reads and edits code and runs commands on our PC. A session can start **subagents** (helpers that each begin with a fresh context) and **workflows** (scripts that run many subagents to a fixed plan).
**Checks and gates.** The test runs and reviews that decide whether a piece of work is good enough to merge into the main line of code.
**Memory.** Whatever carries what we learned from one session to the next: notes, the library we have designed, the knowledge store.

**The token budget.** A **token** is the unit a model reads and writes in, a short piece of text. The **context window** is everything the model holds in mind for one call, and it re-reads the whole window on every call. Our Claude plan allows a limited amount of use in each five-hour window, so tokens are the resource every part of the harness shares.
**The machine.** The one PC everything runs on: its power, memory, disk and Docker (the tool that runs our databases and Linux test runs in containers).
**How results reach me.** Reports, visual pages and decision forms.
p1.sources: Two of our own projects feed this record. **FixFlow** is the workshop management system we are building for a home-appliance repair shop in Karachi: a web app for the manager, an Android app for technicians and a backend in FastAPI (a Python web framework). Its build is laid out in the **ship plan**, the document that orders FixFlow’s work into phases (P0a, P0b and on). **The clinic testbed** is an earlier large build on this same PC that we used to push the harness hard: 432 commits and 65 merges in eight working days [M]. Most of our measured bottlenecks come from its record. Two outside sources were studied card by card: talks and writing by **Dex Horthy** of HumanLayer, and **BAML**, BoundaryML’s language for typed model calls.
p1.arch: On 11 November we put what we had learned into one design, **harness v2**. It treats the harness as one system with four scarce things: time on the check, review, the one-at-a-time merge, and tokens per five-hour window. Each scarce thing gets a part that controls it.
p1.loops: The loop labels come from **system dynamics**, the method Jay Forrester began at MIT in the 1950s for studying systems as stocks, flows and feedback. A reinforcing loop (R) feeds itself: more of it makes more of it. A balancing loop (B) pushes back toward a limit.

p2.lead: A bottleneck is anything that keeps the harness from going faster: a limit it runs into, a step that waits, a defect that slips through, or a decision that waits on me. We ran sessions just to find these and to size them. This part shows what they found, where the biggest ones are and what fixing them would unlock.
p2.classes: The bottleneck compile of 11 November sorted each of its bottlenecks into one of four classes, and the register (our joined list of every bottleneck) keeps them: **Build** (we know the fix and it needs building), **Decide** (it waits on a decision from me), **Diagnose** (we need one measurement to find the cause) and **Trial** (we try a fix and measure it).
p2.shapes: The two projects show the same mechanism in two shapes. The clinic testbed ran **one big window**: its main sessions held 74 % [M] of its tokens at about 333k tokens per call. FixFlow ran **many small windows**: 1,118 agent windows [M] of about 12 calls each. Inside each agent window, 56 % [E] of the tokens was the fixed start every agent re-reads, about 60k tokens [E], most of it the descriptions of tools and connectors (plug-ins that link Claude to outside services).
p2.ruledOut: **Checked and ruled out.** The model mix (routing changes the price per token, not the count), file reads (re-reading a file inside the same window is only 0.5–1.5 % [M]), any one file (the busiest is 1.5 % [M] of its project’s tokens) and my prompts. The usage is in the agents’ own automated steps, which is good news: steps are what we control. **Still to learn:** how re-read tokens count against the plan’s five-hour limit. Until we know, we treat a cut in tokens as a saving in usage and measure separately whether it also means fewer stops.
p2.machine: The first three numbers set the agenda for the first three phases of harness v2; the fourth, the ~70k every agent re-reads, is work for the token budget (phase 5, WP5). The machine comes first because everything stands on it, and its protections are known and cheap: no sleep on mains power, an always-on sensor logger, a resume list that brings sessions back two at a time and a verified copy of the work off the PC. The check comes second because that is where the measured wins already are, and the review rounds come third, as scripts that cost no tokens.

p4.lead: Fifteen packages between them carry every bottleneck in the register and every idea in Part 3. Six can start today, six start the day I give my word, and three follow another package. Read the box under the map before you take one.
p4.packages: One row per package. Each size carries its tag: [E] where a design estimated it, [G] where it is my guess until the first step reports; a package not yet sized says so. Write your name in the owner column when you take one. Two people can share a package; one person should not hold two packages from the same start column (today, on my word, after another package). The reference edition has a full card for each package, with the bottlenecks and ideas it carries and the kind of person it suits.
p4.decisions: Every open decision the package rows name, in one place; go-aheads and permission yeses without an id are in each package’s “Waits on me”. The reference edition gives the options for each and the one the source design recommends. I answered D01 to D06 on 11 November and merged PR #185 on 13 November; only D05’s power-cut notes are still to come.
p4.mapShows: The left column needs no decision from me, no agents and no Docker gate for its first deliverable; the middle column waits on my word and the right one on another package. WP2a’s side-by-side runs need only a quiet machine, so they can start sooner.

howMade: The reference edition came first, following our orchestration design: Sonnet agents extracted every idea, bottleneck and term from the sources with a citation each, without judging them; fresh-context Opus agents checked the records and every number against the sources; nine fresh-context readers read the draft as newcomers. This edition was cut from it: agents condensed the themes, picked the key bottlenecks and shortened the packages, and fresh checkers compared every number and claim with its record. Three more fresh readers (a newcomer, a tone reader and a numbers checker) then read it, and Opus skeptics kept 33 [M] of their 60 [M] findings. Numbers keep their tags. Two things here are newer than the reference edition: PR #185’s merge on 13 November, and the readers’ fixes, such as the graph test’s audited range.

themes.summary: Everything we build runs on one PC that powers off unexpectedly, and the clinic testbed still lives only there. Separate worktrees already pay: when the power went on 13 November, all eight [M] FixFlow lanes resumed from their own copies. Next, WP1 copies the work off the PC nightly, adds a resume list and an always-on sensor logger to find the cause.

key.name: Commit and push at every green checkpoint
key.line: Lanes commit and push at every checkpoint where checks pass, and the gate scripts treat locks older than the last boot as dead. In use since the 28-minute [M] outage.

key.name: Shutdown diagnosis and always-on sensor logger
key.line: Our logs showed 15 of 25 [M] shutdowns since 1 October with no Claude call shortly before, so our load alone does not explain them. The logger is allowed, not yet installed.

key.name: Off-machine copy of the work
key.line: A verified git bundle of every branch plus uncommitted work and transcripts, copied off the PC nightly. Designed; the first copy comes after I plug in the encrypted drive (D02).

themes.summary: The check decides whether work can merge, so it must be fast, fair and never pass when it tested nothing. Running tests in parallel took the clinic check from 855.2 s [M] to 283.8 s [M]; FixFlow’s gate harness uses several of these ideas daily. Next, WP2a runs the container and Windows checks side by side, measuring the peak memory that sizes the check slots.

key.name: Parallel check with one database per worker
key.line: Tests run in parallel workers, each with its own PostgreSQL test database, plus a serial pass for race tests. In use in the testbed: the full check averages 283.8 s [M].

key.name: Skip-aware integration gate
key.line: Integration tests run against the real database; a script fails the gate if any was skipped, so a missing database setting cannot go unnoticed. In use in every FixFlow backend gate run.

key.name: Linux container check, proposed as the gate
key.line: A Linux container runs the check, faster than on Windows, and it found 2 failures [M] Windows missed. Built in the testbed; I decide in D09 whether it becomes the gate.

themes.summary: In the clinic testbed a slice took 2.8 [M] review rounds on average, and in most high-risk merges nobody read the final commit. Opus review already works: it found a serious defect in 9 of 14 [M] Opus-built clinic slices. Next, WP3 moves the mechanical part of review into scripts that spend no tokens, starting with the replay seal and transcript audit.

key.name: Two-level merge gates with refute-reviewers
key.line: The root runs the full check and read-only Opus reviewers try to refute claims. In use for every testbed slice: it caught 19 [M] high-severity (P1) findings in round one.

key.name: Close findings only on tests with positive controls
key.line: A finding closes only on a test the harness runs, and every “nothing found” check needs a case it must find. In use in the testbed; a FixFlow trial is proposed.

key.name: Transcript audit at each merge
key.line: A read-only script over our session transcripts shows whether a reviewer read the final head. Built; its testbed run used 0 [M] model calls. WP3 builds the merge-time version first.

key.name: Fix-round contract: two rounds, revert, test per finding
key.line: Each finding needs a fail-before, pass-after test, and a failed fix is reverted, not patched over. Designed, not yet run; it starts with a replay on recorded fix chains.

themes.summary: More lanes help only up to the knee; past it they add queues, tokens and collisions. Since 13 November FixFlow runs a coordinator session with one lane session per phase, and all eight [M] lanes resumed after a power loss. Next, WP4 replays the plan check on FixFlow’s first lane wave: where lanes would collide and the lane count it would have chosen.

key.name: Lane sessions: one phase, own worktree, run together
key.line: Each lane is an Opus-led session in its own worktree, taking a single phase to a draft PR. In use in FixFlow; RAM, not CPU, sets the lane ceiling [M].

key.name: Per-checkout isolation of worktree, port and database
key.line: Each checkout gets its own worktree, branch, port and database, and a second, simultaneous check of it is refused. In use in the testbed, where it supported 65 merges [M].

key.name: Plan check with footprints and collision graphs
key.line: Each slice declares its footprint, the files it will write; the plan check maps collisions and refuses overlapping writes. Designed in harness v2, not yet run on a real plan.

themes.summary: Almost all our context tokens are re-reads of a window the model already read, so what we manage is calls times window size. Today each phase starts in a fresh session and Opus sessions compact earlier: 38 of 48 [M] compactions came at 366–387k tokens. Next, WP5 proposes the token budget per five-hour window (D07), then puts the four levers to work.

key.name: Earlier auto-compact window
key.line: Compacts sessions earlier so later calls carry a smaller window. In use for Opus; Sonnet sessions ran to 963k [M], and a Sonnet trial waits on my D22.

key.name: One token budget: two lanes at a time
key.line: Two lanes at a time, each step written to disk. In use in the testbed; one five-hour window took about 3.4M [M] subagent tokens, the starting point for my D07 budget figure.

key.name: Strip fixed prefix with a short tool list
key.line: A short tool list, with tool descriptions loaded only when needed, aims to shrink the fixed start every agent re-reads (about 70,000 tokens [M] in the testbed). Designed; D18 waits on a with-and-without test.

themes.summary: Every new session starts without what the last one learned. For state, the repository passed its first test: a fresh agent recovered the facts from it alone. For lessons, the library and the knowledge store are designed, not built; next come the library’s limitation list (WP6a) and the store’s recurrence audit, which counts repeated problems (WP6b).

key.name: Short disciplined notes file as context memory
key.line: A short notes file, kept current and read to resume. Tested in a small, interrupted clinic study: recall 15 of 15 [M], matching both other arms; new mechanisms must beat it.

key.name: Fresh-agent cold-resume trial
key.line: A fresh Sonnet agent must recover frozen facts from the repository alone. Tested once: it recovered 10 of 10 [M] and exposed plan defects to fix; next, re-run at later phases.

key.name: Real-case walkthroughs of the library design
key.line: Agents walked real cases through the library’s design steps. Tested on 59 [M] chosen cases: 69 limitations [M], showing where it breaks, not how often. Next, we agree the list.

key.name: Knowledge store of solved problems (PR #183)
key.line: Stores hard solved problems, traps and failed approaches; a cheap agent looks them up by symptom. Designed, not built; next, the recurrence audit counting repeats (KS-D1), then my build decision (KS-D1b).

themes.summary: Before an agent changes code, it must find what the change touches. In a test on held-out FixFlow commits, with no agent in the loop, the typed code store reached recall 0.700 [M], ahead of scripted search; the gain sits in the mobile app. Next comes the zero-token index replay (WP7), then a test with an agent, once I settle GT-1.

key.name: Typed symbol-level graph of the repo
key.line: A model-free script maps the repo’s symbols and typed links. Tested on held-out commits without an agent: recall 0.700 [M], ahead of scripted search; the gain sits in the mobile app.

key.name: Same-facts cross-check between engines
key.line: Engines given the same facts must agree; a mismatch is a bug. In use: ours agreed on 770 of 770 [M] tasks, so we can choose one on speed, size and effort.

key.name: Agent-in-the-loop pilot
key.line: A fixed agent replays fix commits with and without SQL, graph or BM25 tools, counting tokens and success. An idea, not yet run; it follows the index replay, once I settle GT-1.

themes.summary: Many agents work at once, so briefing, model choice and judging need one written method. Its core is in use: a main session plans and judges, cheaper models discover with citations and fresh-context reviewers try to refute; in one staged run, discovery covered 16/16 [M] areas. Next, WP10a starts with a save-as-run rule: every workflow saved as a script before it runs.

key.name: Staged workflows with judging gates
key.line: Cheap discovery, a judging gate, an Opus deep-dive, another gate, then the phase plan; the main session writes a record at each gate. In use; one deep-dive returned 139 [M] findings.

key.name: Model tiers by role, raise effort before tier
key.line: Haiku extracts, Sonnet maps and runs gates, Opus analyses and refutes, the main session judges. In use in FixFlow and the clinic testbed; cost per tier not yet measured.

key.name: Coordinator session that never implements
key.line: One session owns the plan, shared results and merge calls, dispatches reviews and never implements. In use; it lets 8 [M] lanes run at once; speed effect not yet measured.

key.name: Save-rule and run provenance
key.line: Each evidence folder keeps the workflow script as it ran and its arguments, so the run can be repeated and audited. Designed, not yet tested; WP10a writes the rule first.

themes.summary: A subagent inherits the session’s model and loads nothing unless told, so a simple lookup can run on our most expensive tier. Our skill packages and pinned FixFlow agents are merged (PR #185) but not yet run; in use today is local GPU transcription of talks, at 19–45× real time [M]. Next, WP10b adds a frontmatter CI check and tallies which skills fire.

key.name: Agent file: pinned model, tools, preloaded skill
key.line: Each agent file pins its model, tools and preloaded skill; the agent works read-only unless told and cites everything. Built: 11 fixflow agent definitions [M], merged 13 November; not yet run.

key.name: [owner] stop markers in agent procedures
key.line: Steps only I may do, such as deploys or live restores, carry an [owner] marker; the agent stops and hands me the exact command. Built into all 13 skills [M], untested.

key.name: CI check for skill and agent frontmatter
key.line: A Node CI step fails bad skill and agent frontmatter, such as a name that differs from its folder. Designed, not built; WP10b first runs it record-only, flagging without blocking.

themes.summary: To choose fixes we need numbers we can trust and tests that are fair to the idea they test. Every number in our program documents carries a tag for how sure we are, and a transcript tally found that, by one count, slice sessions used 66.4 % [M] of November’s tokens. Next, WP8 builds a tagged rate sheet from the record.

key.name: Token tally from session transcripts
key.line: Read-only scripts parse every session transcript, count each call once, and total tokens and compactions per group. Measured for October and November; a re-measurement agreed within 0.3 % [M].

key.name: Pre-registered, sealed held-out test protocol
key.line: Freeze the test sets, metric and smallest worthwhile difference before any arm exists. In use on the graph test; every arm lost 0.05 to 0.17 [M] recall from tuning to held-out.

key.name: Measured-rates table feeding planner and governor
key.line: Measured rates, such as check time and rounds per slice, updated each wave for the planner and governor. Designed, not yet tested; WP8 starts it, writing unknowns as unknown.

themes.summary: In the clinic testbed, first-use gaps hid behind test data until the last day; nothing ran on a real host. The testbed’s local staging rig already rehearses deploy and restore on synthetic data, with a fresh virtual machine serving in 109 s [M]; FixFlow’s lab emulator boots on this PC. Next, WP9 adds a zero-seed walk to every gate, then a real-host rehearsal.

key.name: Local staging VM rig with drills
key.line: A script-built Debian virtual machine with re-runnable drills: deploy, upgrade, backup and restore, load, security probe. In use in the testbed on synthetic data; next, a fresh-VM restore with me present.

key.name: Volume load and page-speed drill
key.line: Times pages on growing synthetic data and fingerprints each page to prove a speed-up changed no figures. Measured in the testbed: slow pages fell to 0.1–0.5 s [M]; next, a load rerun.

key.name: Zero-seed first-use walk in every gate
key.line: On an empty database, each gate walks install, first user, tills, a real-shaped import, a transaction and close of day. Designed, not built; would add 2 to 3 minutes [E] per gate.

themes.summary: Work waits on my decisions, and I decide quickly when I can see the choice on one page. In use today: W0-results.md, our single working board, which tracked 8 running lanes [M] on 13 November, and decision cards that mark the option the design recommends. Next, WP11 joins every open decision into one board beside the shared run queue.

key.name: W0-results.md as the single working board
key.line: One file holds my P0a steps, my decisions with defaults and the lane board; unknowns are written as unknown, with the reason. In use in FixFlow.

key.name: Decision cards D01 to D23
key.line: Each card shows the options, the one the design recommends, the bottlenecks touched and my answer. In use: D01 to D06 are answered; D07, the token budget, follows P0a.

key.name: Ship plan first; my yes for outside actions
key.line: FixFlow’s P0a goes first; no hooks, installs, scheduled tasks, permission changes or outbound data without my decision, and no harness agents during a FixFlow phase. Adopted as a standing rule.

picks.name: The PC powers off without warning
picks.big: 24 power-offs, 7 Oct–10 Nov, 23 without crash code [M]; on 13 Nov a 28-minute outage cut eight lanes [M].
picks.unlocks: Next power-off names its cause; zero sleep-related events in 14 days [T]; every stop is cheap to recover.

picks.name: Usage limits stop every lane at once
picks.big: 14 limit episodes, 6–20 Oct [M]; ten lanes were stopped by the limit within about 15 minutes [M].
picks.unlocks: A governor slows lanes so the usage window lasts; resumes never pay again for finished agents.

picks.name: Memory is short on this PC
picks.big: Memory, not CPU, caps check slots and lanes; on 13 Nov FixFlow had 5.5–7.7 of 31 GB free with eight lanes [M].
picks.unlocks: Slot and lane counts from a table of who holds memory when under 2 GB [T] is free.

picks.name: Checks queue behind each other
picks.big: 19 recorded waits: median 409 s, longest 2,030 s [M]; a second slot’s 8 GiB never free in about 980 samples [M].
picks.unlocks: Median wait under a minute [T] and up to 1.8–1.9× check throughput [M] with a second slot.

picks.name: Fix rounds that create new defects
picks.big: 64 % of reviews sent a slice back, 2.8 rounds per slice [M]; fixes made at least 5 more P1 defects [M].
picks.unlocks: Review rounds that converge under a stop rule, with fewer new defects per finding fixed.

picks.name: Agent reports overstate what was done
picks.big: 20-plus recorded overstatements of tests, evidence or runs [M]; model re-checks did not stop them.
picks.unlocks: Claims a script can recheck, with false flags under 10 % [T]; the orchestrator stops re-verifying by hand.

picks.name: Final commits not yet read by a person
picks.big: All review is a model reading a model’s code; 5 of 6 high-risk final commits went unread [M].
picks.unlocks: Unread high-risk merges cut from 5 of 6 [M] to zero [T].

picks.name: One orchestrator is the serial gate
picks.big: One root session reviews, merges and runs checks, capping how fast work leaves; it took 15.3 % of November tokens [M].
picks.unlocks: No compaction across a wave of five gates [T]; the token gain is bounded by that share.

picks.name: Code phases waited on my P0a
picks.big: 37 of 56 phases wait behind P0a [M]; on 13 Nov production still answered Railway’s edge 404 [M].
picks.unlocks: Finishing P0a unblocks all work that reaches a phone or host; lanes build ahead until then.

picks.name: Work waits for me when I am away
picks.big: Restarts wait for me: Docker and sessions stay down; about three days idle after the 6 Nov power-off [M].
picks.unlocks: Time from “could resume” to next commit falls from about three days [M] to under three hours [T].

picks.name: Gaps found only on the last day
picks.big: Every clinic slice was tested on synthetic data; two [M] first-use gaps surfaced only on the final day.
picks.unlocks: First-use failures caught at every gate, not on the last day, by a zero-seed walk.

picks.name: Context growth in long sessions
picks.big: Slice sessions took 66.4 % [M] of cache reads at about 306k [M] per call; a Sonnet window reached 963k [M].
picks.unlocks: Capping windows at 150–200k [T], with one phase per session, targets our largest exposure.

picks.name: Fixed start-up cost per agent
picks.big: Every agent re-reads its fixed start on every call: about 70k [M] in the clinic testbed, about 60k [E] in FixFlow; 27 % [E] of all tokens, 47 % [E] of FixFlow’s.
picks.unlocks: Deferred schemas, fewer connectors and no skills in agent sessions would remove most of it.

picks.name: Library reuse funnel: where work drops out
picks.big: Modelled at middle values: of 100 pieces the cheap model gets wrong, 0.35 [G] end right; most unknowns are guesses.
picks.unlocks: At the all-good setting, 31.7 [G] of 100 end right: the prize if every step holds.

picks.name: Hard problems re-solved at the top tier
picks.big: Past diagnoses live only as prose, unsearchable by symptom; 3 to 5 [M] same-cause repeats among 48 [M] fix commits on main.
picks.unlocks: A cheap agent finds, checks and reuses a recorded fix instead of Fable or Opus re-solving it.

picks.name: Context aids not yet run with an agent
picks.big: 0 [M] agent runs: the graph test used a fixed search script; a quality comparison was forecast at 156M–512M [E] tokens.
picks.unlocks: Answers my real question: whether a graph, map or recall layer saves an agent work.

rows.goal: No power-off costs us work or a day: a nightly off-machine copy, a resume list and a sensor logger.
rows.first: Bundle-and-verify and nightly copy scripts, covering uncommitted work (B11); first verified copy after my drive step; my steps follow P0a.
rows.done: Copy verified, never over 24 hours old [T]; after a reboot, resume list shown, databases healthy within 3 minutes [T]; shutdowns leave logger traces.
rows.waits: Sleep-off (D04), drive (D02) and logger (D05) steps, copy and Railway-rule yeses; D08 later.

rows.goal: One fast, fair, visible check for the clinic testbed: a Linux container gate, memory-sized slots, a queue, heartbeat and reaper.
rows.first: Side-by-side container and Windows runs, one check’s peak memory [M]; a quiet machine suffices. Memory table and second slot wait for WP1.
rows.done: Median gate near 230 s [T]; zero Linux-only failures on main; heartbeat gaps within 60 s [T]; a stall names its test; leftovers cleared.
rows.waits: D09 (container gate), D10 (what may be cleaned), later D11 (who gives up memory).

rows.goal: Keep FixFlow’s gates and slot lock fast, fair and honest; CI fails when it should, never passing an empty run.
rows.first: Per-lane gate waits measured under the ticket queue, and proof that CI fails on skipped integration tests and empty Jest runs.
rows.done: Every gate locks per lane first; Node failures re-run under Node 22; a planted skip or empty run turns CI red, after record-only runs.
rows.waits: My go, through the coordinator, before any change to `ff-gates.sh` or `ff-slot.sh`.

rows.goal: Move the mechanical part of review and merging out of the orchestrator into scripts that spend no tokens.
rows.first: Replay seal and transcript audit on recorded data, at no token cost; seal tests run under D07; verdict script easier after WP2a.
rows.done: Each script passes its harness v2 test; the merge queue, record-only over 65 [M] recorded merges, flags unread final heads; no refusals before D15.
rows.waits: D12 to D20 as each mechanism reaches me; D13 and D17 are permission changes.

rows.goal: Know before a wave which slices can run side by side, how many lanes pay, and where they would collide.
rows.first: The plan check replayed on FixFlow’s first lane wave: its collision graph and lane count. Needs WP8’s rate sheet; easier after WP2a.
rows.done: Runs record-only on the next wave first; sets the lane count only after the coordinator and I accept it.
rows.waits: Accepting its recommendation, with the coordinator.

rows.goal: Give every wave a written token budget and a governor so the five-hour window lasts; apply the token report’s levers.
rows.first: A D07 budget proposal from the November tally, at no token cost; the fixed-start and lookup levers wait for WP3 and D18.
rows.done: Every wave launches with a written budget, agents booked in the shared queue; each lever has a before-and-after number; none claims fewer limit stops.
rows.waits: D07 budget, D13 reports folder, D18 tool list, D22 trial; yes before removing connectors.

rows.goal: Give the harness a memory a cheaper model can use, asked for, never pushed; limitations agreed before any fix.
rows.first: The limitation list agreed with me, each with its alone and last weights; the pilot needs WP8’s frozen validation contract and protocol.
rows.done: A held-out pilot, under the frozen validation contract, measures whether asking the library first means reading less and getting more right.
rows.waits: Agreeing the limitation list (LIB); pilot agent runs wait for D07.

rows.goal: If the audit says it pays, build PR #183’s knowledge store: solved hard problems and traps, looked up on demand.
rows.first: Recurrence audit (KS-0), no code: counts repeats a store could have served. Runs under D07 in a quiet window; pilots need WP8.
rows.done: Audit reported; if built, pilot recall at shown 60 % or more [T], zero acted-on false positives [T], every planted forbidden diff caught [T].
rows.waits: KS-D1 (audit), KS-D1b (build), D17 (hooks), my yes before a copy leaves this PC.

rows.goal: Make our documents fail a check when they drift from the code, starting with the facts CLAUDE.md states.
rows.first: Alembic-head CI check for CLAUDE.md and one corrections PR for PR #183’s listed contradictions; lands after the ship phase in flight.
rows.done: A planted wrong fact in CLAUDE.md turns CI red, after record-only runs over recent merges, and the corrections PR has merged.
rows.waits: My go through the coordinator, and the merge.

rows.goal: A fast, trustworthy answer to “what does this change touch?”: the typed code store, indexes and the wider graph test.
rows.first: Index replay at no token cost on recorded windows, once D23 sets its marks; the agent arm needs WP8’s pre-registered protocol.
rows.done: Index replay reported against D23’s marks; if GT-1 is approved, a tested answer: does the typed store beat search alone on speed and tokens?
rows.waits: D23 (what the replay must show), GT-1 agent pilot, GT-2 installs, D07 for agents.

rows.goal: Keep the numbers every package depends on and the rules that keep tests fair: rates, the frozen validation contract, protocols.
rows.first: Rate sheet from the record (check time, review rounds, send-backs, limit episodes), each tagged, gaps marked unknown; commit only on my word.
rows.done: Rate sheet updated each wave, every rate tagged; contract and protocols written before any pilot; WP4 and WP5 read their rates there.

rows.goal: Find the last-day gaps on day one: a zero-seed walk in every gate, a real-host rehearsal and a load-drill rerun.
rows.first: The zero-seed walk (install to close of day, fresh database) as a gate step; needs WP2a’s container gate first.
rows.done: The walk fails before the 11 November real-data merge (fb55599) and passes after; the first-deploy checklist has run once on a real host.
rows.waits: D21 (rehearse on a real host; renting one needs my yes), D09 via WP2a.

rows.goal: Brief and run agents well: brief contracts, judgement-free discovery with citations, fresh-context skeptics, saved workflows, state on disk.
rows.first: The save-as-run rule, sent to the coordinator, and one saved review-stage workflow script; agent launches wait for D07.
rows.done: Every workflow we run is saved and re-runnable, raw outputs kept with their hashes, and WP3’s sealed replay catches verdict-flipping brief edits.

rows.goal: Give agents tested domain skills: PR #185’s skills and FixFlow agents, merged on 13 November, each with a pinned model and short tool list.
rows.first: A frontmatter CI check, proposed to the coordinator and run record-only first.
rows.done: A trigger tally shows which skills fire; lookups run on the pinned cheaper agents, with token use compared against the built-in agent’s.
rows.waits: My go on the CI check through the coordinator; agent runs for the tally wait for D07.

rows.goal: Keep me deciding quickly and seeing clearly: one board for every open decision, readable pages and a current compile.
rows.first: One decision board (D01 to D23, KS-D, graph-test decisions, links to my FixFlow items) and the shared run queue beside it.
rows.done: No package waits more than a day [T] on a decision of mine, with each wait logged.
rows.waits: Answering the board; “accept all defaults” covers only free decisions staying on this PC.

before.title: Two projects, one PC: the ship plan first
before.text: Work on a branch, never on main, and never delay or edit FixFlow’s next phase for harness work. Before using the Docker gate or an agent, read the lane board (`docs/program/W0-results.md`) on PR #182’s plan branch: FixFlow phases running or awaiting review go first, as they share this PC’s memory and our usage limit.

before.title: One budget for the whole team
before.text: Two lanes at a time (your own session counts), a written token budget before any launch (D07) and one agent-adding change per five-hour window, shared by everyone. Stop launching after the first empty result, a possible usage limit. Book agent runs in WP11’s shared queue; until it exists, wait for my yes.

before.title: One limit on heavy checks
before.text: A heavy check from either project takes a slot from `ff-slot.sh`, FixFlow’s machine-wide lock. Its pools and slot counts stay as they are; WP2b may propose only how waiters are ordered.

before.title: The coordinator writes FixFlow’s program files
before.text: Changes to the ship plan, lane board or FixFlow’s gate scripts go to the coordinator as proposals; the coordinator brings them to me and writes them once I say go.

before.title: Machine traps that already cost us time
before.text: Never prune Docker networks or restart Docker; new networks get explicit subnets inside 10.77.0.0/16. Under `MSYS_NO_PATHCONV`, write `C:/…` paths. Clone with `core.longpaths`. No `python` on PATH; use Node. Never touch the antivirus.
